claims.text: The initial eutectic HEA has a disordered FCC matrix and ordered B2 precipitates.
The initial alloy has high stacking-fault energy and a homogeneous elemental distribution.
Aging at approximately 600–800 °C nucleates and grows local chemical orders within the FCC phase.
Aging in this range does not cause significant grain coarsening or impurity segregation.
A lack of intergranular fracture verifies the absence of grain-boundary embrittlement.
Aging produces nanoscale, coherent, ordered clusters within the FCC matrix.
The ordered clusters increase lattice friction and act as strong dislocation-pinning points.
The ordered clusters locally reduce the stacking-fault energy.
Molecular-dynamics simulations of CoNiCrFeMn nanowires found that friction arising from constituent-atom lattice-parameter differences hinders partial-dislocation motion.
Severe local lattice distortion can impede dislocation motion and produce pronounced strengthening in HEAs.
The LCO-induced frictional barrier impedes dislocation cross-slip and forces dislocations into planar arrays.
Planar slip localization produces localized strain and premature brittle fracture.
At higher aging temperatures, LCOs dissolve or coarsen beyond an effective pinning size.
LCO dissolution or over-coarsening permits dislocations to bypass the clusters by cross-slip or climb, restoring ductility.
Ductility will decrease sharply at intermediate aging conditions and recover at higher aging temperatures or longer aging states.
Fracture in the transient brittle regime will be transgranular and associated with planar slip bands rather than intergranular separation.
Classical impurity-segregation or grain-coarsening models predict monotonic degradation or recovery governed by grain-boundary area.
The embrittlement regime exists while LCOs are thermodynamically stable and kinetically able to form coherent interfaces, but before grain growth or secondary-phase coarsening dominates.
Persistence of embrittlement when APT shows no LCOs, or exclusively intergranular fracture without planar slip bands, would falsify the LCO mechanism.
Rapid quenching after aging can prevent LCO formation while leaving grain boundaries pristine.

contradictions.description: The intervention states that LCOs nucleate and grow during aging, whereas the falsification rule suggests that rapid quenching after the aging treatment can prevent their formation. Quenching after LCO-forming aging would ordinarily preserve already formed order rather than prevent its formation unless the aging protocol itself is changed.
